lead: Language is not one flat string of words. It is built in layers. Each layer has its own unit and answers its own question. Speech sounds form words; words form phrases and sentences; sentences carry literal meaning; meaning changes with context. NLP systems copy this order because a wrong choice low down corrupts every layer above. Search, translation, voice assistants and chatbots all depend on these layers. The five levels are named here, one sentence is read at each, and the order explains why errors spread.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the applications that each level serves.

sections.h3: The five layers and their units

blocks.text: Start at the bottom. Phonetics studies speech sounds as physical events. Phonology studies the sound units, called phonemes, that distinguish one word from another in a language. The unit is the phoneme; the question is “which sounds matter here?” Morphology studies how words are built from morphemes, the smallest meaning-bearing pieces. pay plus a past-tense morpheme gives paid, an irregular surface form. The unit is the morpheme; the question is “what is this word made of?” Syntax groups words into phrases and sentences and fixes word order. The unit is the phrase or sentence; the question is “what goes with what?” Semantics assigns literal meaning to words and sentences. The unit is the word sense or the sentence meaning; the question is “what does this literally say?” Pragmatics studies meaning in context: speaker intent, implied meaning and speech acts such as request or report. Discourse extends this across sentences. The unit is the utterance in context; the question is “what is the speaker doing and what is left unsaid?” Some syllabi call this set the levels of linguistic analysis. Higher layers use the output of lower layers, as the figure shows.

sections.h3: Higher layers depend on lower ones

blocks.text: The dependency is strict in one direction. Syntax cannot group words until tokenization and morphology give it words with part-of-speech guesses. Semantics cannot choose the right sense of bank until syntax says it is a noun and shows the phrase it sits in. Pragmatics cannot infer intent until semantics gives a literal meaning to reject or extend. Discourse cannot resolve it until earlier sentences and syntax give possible antecedents. A lower-level mistake therefore spreads upward. If paid is tagged as a noun, syntax may look for a subject after it. If Anna Salai is split into two tokens, the parser may see two places. If the bill is attached to bank instead of paid, the literal meaning changes. Higher context can sometimes repair a lower error, but not reliably.

Ambiguity is local at each level. Phonology: read has two pronunciations. Morphology: unlockable can mean able to be unlocked or not lockable. Syntax: I saw the man with the telescope has two attachments. Semantics: bank has several senses. Pragmatics: Can you pass the salt? is a request, not a yes/no question.

An NLP pipeline follows the layers. First normalize and tokenize the raw text (Chapter 1.4). Next assign morphology and lemma (Chapter 1.5, Chapter 1.6). Then tag parts of speech and build syntax; Unit 2 and Unit 3 cover these steps. Then assign literal meaning and word senses; Unit 4 covers this. Finally use context, discourse and intent. The order is not decoration. A wrong token changes the lemma; a wrong lemma changes the part of speech; a wrong part of speech changes the parse; a wrong parse changes the meaning. In a Chennai power-cut message, current must become the electricity sense, not a river current. That choice needs sentence context, but it also needs correct tokenization and a noun tag. Most system errors are not deep reasoning failures. They are lower-layer decisions made once and never checked.

spec.aria: A five-layer pyramid from phonology at the base to pragmatics at the top, with worked-sentence notes: Ravi has 2 syllables, paid has 2 morphemes, syntax has 2 prep phrases, bill means amount owed, and the sentence reports a past event.

examples.question: Annotate the sentence Ravi paid the bill at the bank near Anna Salai at each of the five levels. State the number of morphemes in paid and the number of prepositional phrases in the syntax.
steps: Phonology: Ravi has two syllables. paid ends in the sound /d/; bank has the sounds /bæŋk/. The article the is pronounced /ðə/ before the consonant sounds in bill and bank. English also has /ðiː/ before vowel sounds, but it is not used here.

Morphology: Ravi is one free morpheme. For this annotation, paid is the verb stem pay plus a past-tense morpheme, realized irregularly as paid; count 2 morphemes. the, bill, at, bank and near are single free morphemes. Anna Salai is a proper name.

Syntax: subject noun phrase Ravi; verb paid; object noun phrase the bill; prepositional phrase at the bank; inside that noun phrase, prepositional phrase near Anna Salai. Count 2 prepositional phrases.

Semantics: bill means an amount owed, not a bird beak or a proposed law. bank means a financial building, not a river side. Literal meaning: Ravi settled an amount owed at a financial building located near Anna Salai.
Pragmatics: the sentence reports a past event and informs the listener. The listener is expected to know which bank is meant, or to infer it from Anna Salai. It is not a question or a request.
examples.answer: The sentence is annotated at all five levels; paid has 2 morphemes and the syntax has 2 prepositional phrases.
examples.check:
levels = 5
morphemes_paid = 2
prepositional_phrases = 2
print(levels)
print(morphemes_paid)
print(prepositional_phrases)

traps: Do not put syntax below morphology. Word-internal structure is morphology; phrase structure is syntax.
Do not call pragmatics only politeness. It covers intent, context, implied meaning and speech acts.
Do not confuse phonetics with phonology. Phonetics is physical sound; phonology is the sound system that distinguishes words.
Do not expect a higher layer to repair a lower-layer error. A wrong token or lemma usually survives to the final answer.
Do not treat semantics as context-dependent. Literal meaning is semantics; what the speaker means here is pragmatics.

quiz.q: List the five levels from bottom to top and give one unit for each.
quiz.a: Phonology: phoneme; morphology: morpheme; syntax: phrase or sentence; semantics: word sense or sentence meaning; pragmatics: utterance in context.

quiz.q: Why can syntax not be done before morphology?
quiz.a: Syntax needs words and their categories. Morphology supplies word structure and helps decide whether a form is a noun, verb or adjective, so a wrong lemma or tag changes the phrase structure.

quiz.q: In Can you open the window?, which level gives the literal yes/no question and which gives the request?
quiz.a: Semantics gives the literal question about ability. Pragmatics gives the request to open the window.

quiz.q: A tagger labels paid as a noun. Trace one likely syntax error and one likely semantics error.
quiz.a: Syntax may treat paid as the head of a noun phrase and look for a verb elsewhere, so the subject-verb-object grouping breaks. Semantics may read paid as a noun rather than a past action, so the event meaning is lost.

quiz.q: What is the difference between semantics and pragmatics?
quiz.a: Semantics is literal meaning. Pragmatics is meaning in context: speaker intent, implied meaning and speech acts.

quiz.q: The word bank appears in river bank and money bank. Which level chooses the sense, and what lower-level information does it use?
quiz.a: Semantics chooses the sense. It uses the noun tag and the neighbouring words from syntax and morphology: river selects the land sense, money selects the financial sense.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, this layered view becomes an annotation scheme: separate labels for tokens, lemmas, parts of speech, senses and dialogue acts. Error analysis usually starts at the lowest layer that is wrong. Research in large language models asks whether one network learns all layers implicitly, but evaluation still reports them separately. Search next for “levels of linguistic analysis”, “speech acts”, “implicature” and “discourse coherence”.
